knowledge:
- key_parameters: graph=An igraph object representing the network ;; method=The diffusion scoring method to use (e.g., "raw", "ml", "gm", "ber_s", "ber_p", "mc", "z") ;; scores=A named vector or matrix of input scores with node names ;; K=A precomputed dense graph kernel matrix to avoid redundant calculations on medium/large networks ;; validation=A matrix or vector of target labels used to evaluate the performance of the diffusion scores ;; grid_param=A data frame of parameter combinations (e.g., created by expand.grid) for screening multiple methods ;; n.perm=The number of permutations for permutation-based scores (mc, ber_p) or performance evaluation
- alternatives: RANKS=An R package containing a variety of diffusion kernels and kernelised scores for binary input vectors, modeling label propagation as a semi-supervised one-class classification problem ;; HotNet=Uses a diffusion process with mutated genes as seed nodes to find mutated pathways ;; TieDIE=Runs two diffusion processes to link genomic perturbations with transcriptional states ;; GeneMANIA=A label propagation algorithm that introduces a bias term on unlabelled nodes
- when_to_use: Use this package when you have a biological network (e.g., protein-protein interaction network) and a set of node labels (e.g., disease genes, pathways, or differential expression values) and want to propagate these labels to prioritize novel candidates or find functional modules.
- pitfalls: scale_limitations=Explicit kernel computation scales quadratically in memory and is best suited for networks under 20,000 nodes on standard workstations ;; quantitative_inputs=Only raw, ber_s, z, ber_p, and mc accept quantitative inputs; ml and gm are strictly binary. Quantitative inputs must be monotonic (one-tailed) as opposing signs cancel out ;; unlabelled_vs_negatives=In permutation-based scores (mc, ber_p), negatives and unlabelled nodes are not equivalent because only observed nodes are permuted ;; high_positives_slowdown=Stochastic permutation analysis (mc, ber_p) can be slow if the input has a very high number of positive labels; use the parametric z-score as a faster alternative

workflows.name: single_network_diffusion
workflows.intent: Propagate node labels over a network using a specific diffusion method to prioritize candidates and visualize the smoothed scores.
input: node_scores.csv (a named vector or matrix of initial node labels/scores)
workflows.stages:
1. Load the network and input scores.
2. Run diffusion using the diffuse function with a specified method (e.g., "raw" or "mc").
3. Map scores to colors and shapes using scores2colours and scores2shapes for network visualization.
workflows.code:
output_vec <- diffuStats::diffuse(
    graph = graph_toy,
    method = "raw",
    scores = input_vec)

igraph::plot.igraph(
    graph_toy, 
    vertex.color = diffuStats::scores2colours(output_vec),
    vertex.shape = diffuStats::scores2shapes(input_vec),
    main = "Diffusion scores in our lattice"
)

output_mc <- diffuStats::diffuse(
    graph = graph_toy, 
    method = "mc", 
    scores = input_mat)

workflows.name: grid_diffusion_and_benchmarking
workflows.intent: Precompute a graph kernel, run multiple diffusion methods in parallel, and evaluate their performance against validation labels.
input: training_labels.csv (matrix of known node labels for training)
validation_labels.csv (matrix of target node labels for validation)
workflows.stages:
1. Precompute the regularised Laplacian kernel using regularisedLaplacianKernel.
2. Run diffusion across a grid of methods using diffuse_grid.
3. Evaluate performance (e.g., AUROC) of multiple methods using perf.
4. Statistically compare performance metrics using perf_wilcox.
workflows.code:
K_rl <- diffuStats::regularisedLaplacianKernel(yeast)

df_diff <- diffuse_grid(
    K = K_rl,
    scores = scores_A,
    grid_param = expand.grid(method = list_methods),
    n.perm = 1000 
)

df_methods <- perf(
    K = K_rl,
    scores = mat_classes[known, ],
    validation = mat_classes[target, ],
    grid_param = expand.grid(
        method = list_methods,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
    n.perm = 1000
)

df_perf <- reshape2::acast(df_methods, Column~method, value.var = "auc")

df_test <- perf_wilcox(
    df_perf, 
    digits_p = 1, 
    adjust = function(p) p.adjust(p, method = "fdr"), 
    scientific = FALSE)
